images.title: Same unit, then compare
images.purpose: Show the one idea the student practises: recut two bars of the same whole into the same unit, then see which shading reaches further.
images.composition: Two long bars stacked with wide space between them, left edges aligned, and one comparison line centred below.
images.exact_structure: Top: one long bar cut by thin lines into 15 equal cells, with thicker lines after every 3 cells marking fifths; the first 6 cells filled teal #0072B2 from the left. Below: one bar of exactly the same length, left edges aligned, cut into 15 equal cells, with thicker lines after every 5 cells marking thirds; the first 5 cells filled amber #E69F00 from the left. One thin dashed reddish purple #CC79A7 vertical edge line at the end of the teal fill, crossing both bars. Centred below: one comparison line. Exactly 2 bars, 15 cells each, 6 teal, 5 amber.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
any controls, menus or screen elements drawn in the frame
images.takeaway: Cut both wholes into the same unit, then the longer shading is the bigger fraction.
images.description: Two same-length bars both cut into 15 equal cells: 6 teal cells show 2/5 = 6/15 and 5 amber cells show 1/3 = 5/15, and the edge line shows 2/5 > 1/3.
images.context: Shown with the doer concept before the student practises. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not generated yet.
images.teaching_notes: Ask the student to say why 15 works for both fifths and thirds before reading the comparison line.

image_decisions.why: One clean picture of two bars in a common unit sets up the comparing practice.
